items.title: Improving mathematical reasoning with process supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new approach in training mathematical problem-solving models involves rewarding each correct reasoning step, known as process supervision, rather than only the final correct answer. This method not only improves performance but also aligns the model's reasoning process with human-endorsed chains of thought.

items.title: Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers are developing a framework to assess the potential risk of large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4 being used to assist in creating biological threats. An evaluation involving biology experts and students indicated that GPT-4 offers only a slight improvement in accuracy for biological threat creation, which is not significant enough to draw definitive conclusions. This work serves as an initial step for ongoing research and discussions within the community.

items.title: AI and compute [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: We're releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore's Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it's worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today's capabilities.

items.title: More on Dota 2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Our Dota 2 result shows that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

items.content_text: We've found that self-play allows simulated AIs to discover physical skills like tackling, ducking, faking, kicking, catching, and diving for the ball, without explicitly designing an environment with these skills in mind. Self-play ensures that the environment is always the right difficulty for an AI to improve. Taken alongside our Dota 2 self-play results, we have increasing confidence that self-play will be a core part of powerful AI systems in the future.

items.title: Forecasting potential misuses of language models for disinformation campaigns and how to reduce risk [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI researchers collaborated with Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology and the Stanford Internet Observatory to investigate how large language models might be misused for disinformation purposes. The collaboration included an October 2021 workshop bringing together 30 disinformation researchers, machine learning experts, and policy analysts, and culminated in a co-authored report building on more than a year of research. This report outlines the threats that language models pose to the information environment if used to augment disinformation campaigns and introduces a framework for analyzing potential mitigations. Read the full report here.

items.title: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: We've written a policy research paper identifying four strategies that can be used today to improve the likelihood of long-term industry cooperation on safety norms in AI: communicating risks and benefits, technical collaboration, increased transparency, and incentivizing standards. Our analysis shows that industry cooperation on safety will be instrumental in ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial, but competitive pressures could lead to a collective action problem, potentially causing AI companies to under-invest in safety. We hope these strategies will encourage greater cooperation on the safe development of AI and lead to better global outcomes of AI.

items.title: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: We've developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.
